title: Rollback & Safe Deploys
summary: A deploy you can't undo is a bet you can't take back. Learn the deploy-risk equation, health-gated automated rollback, and why database migrations are the part that actually resists rolling back.

slides.markdown:
Every deploy is a bet that the new code is better than the old. Safe deploys aren't about never losing that bet — they're about **losing small and recovering fast** when you do.

That comes down to three levers: limiting how much traffic is exposed before you know (blast radius), noticing something's wrong quickly (detection time), and being able to undo it fast (rollback time). This topic covers each lever, and the one case where "just roll back" doesn't actually work — once a database migration has run and new data has been written against the new schema.

slides.subTitle: Blast radius × detection time × rollback time
slides.markdown:
The actual damage from a bad deploy is roughly the product of three things:

- **Blast radius** — how much traffic/data the bad code touches before you intervene (1% canary vs 100% instant rollout).
- **Detection time** — how long until you know something's wrong (automated alert in 30 seconds vs a customer complaint in 3 hours).
- **Rollback time** — how long until the bad code stops running (a flag flip in seconds vs a full redeploy in 20 minutes).

Every technique in this topic — canaries, health checks, automated rollback triggers — is reducible to shrinking one of these three factors. A team obsessing over one (say, an elaborate canary process) while ignoring another (no alerting, so detection takes hours) hasn't actually reduced risk much.

A **readiness probe** asks "is this instance ready to receive traffic right now?" — checked before the load balancer routes anything to it, and again continuously. A **liveness probe** asks "is this instance still healthy, or should it be restarted?"

During a deploy, readiness probes are what prevent a newly-started instance from receiving traffic before it's finished initializing (warming caches, establishing DB connections) — without one, the first requests to a fresh instance fail while it's still starting up. Liveness probes catch an instance that's alive but stuck (deadlocked, wedged) and restart it automatically, rather than leaving it silently serving errors until a human notices.

Both are cheap, automated detection-time reducers — the second lever in the risk equation.

Rather than waiting for a human to notice a dashboard trending wrong, an automated rollback trigger watches a small set of guardrail metrics — error rate, p99 latency, a key business metric — during and immediately after a deploy, and reverts automatically if any crosses a pre-set threshold.

The reason this beats a human watching: it removes the detection-time lag entirely for the common case, and it removes the judgment call under pressure ("is this blip real or noise?") by deciding the threshold calmly, in advance, rather than live during a possible incident. The trade-off is false positives — too tight a threshold triggers rollback on normal noise, which erodes trust in the automation and gets it disabled exactly when it's needed.

slides.sectionTitle: A deploy pipeline with an abort-and-rollback step
slides.markdown:
<<< Image: a horizontal pipeline diagram — Deploy new version (small %) -> Monitor metrics (a gauge icon, 5-minute window) -> a decision diamond "metrics within threshold?" -> Yes continues to "Increase rollout %", No branches to "Automatic rollback" which routes back to the prior stable version, with a notification icon alerting on-call either way >>>

The key property this diagram is making concrete: the decision to proceed or roll back is **automatic and metric-driven**, not "deploy and wait for someone to complain." The monitoring window is a fixed, short duration — long enough to catch a real regression, short enough that a good deploy isn't stuck waiting unnecessarily.

Rolling back application code is comparatively easy — redeploy the previous artifact or flip a flag. Rolling back a **schema migration** is a different problem, because the moment new rows are written under the new schema, the old application code may no longer understand the data.

Concretely: you add a `NOT NULL` column, deploy new code that writes it, then need to roll back the app due to an unrelated bug. The old code was never written expecting that column, and if it tries to insert a row without it, the insert fails against the NOT NULL constraint. The schema and the application version are now coupled in a way plain "redeploy the old artifact" doesn't undo.

The pattern that keeps schema changes rollback-safe is **expand/contract**, splitting one migration into safe steps:

1. **Expand** — add the new column/table as nullable or with a default; old code ignores it, new code can start using it. Both app versions run fine against this schema.
2. **Migrate** — deploy new code that writes to (and optionally backfills) the new shape, while both old and new code remain compatible with the schema.
3. **Contract** — only after the new code has been running successfully for a while (no rollback plan needed anymore), a *later* migration removes the old column/constraint.

The rule this produces: **never make app-code rollback depend on a schema rollback.** At every point during the rollout, both the old and new app version must be able to run against whatever the current schema is.

slides.subTitle: When rolling back isn't actually safe
slides.markdown:
| | Rollback | Forward-fix |
|---|---|---|
| **Best when** | Bug is in code only, no incompatible data written yet | Data has already been written that the old version can't handle |
| **Speed** | Usually faster — revert to known-good | Slower — requires writing and shipping a real fix |
| **Risk** | Can corrupt state if data shape has moved on | Bug stays live slightly longer, but avoids a worse data-consistency problem |

Once a new version has written data the old version doesn't understand — a new required field, a changed serialization format, a value in a new enum state — rolling back can be **more dangerous than the original bug**, because the old code may now mishandle that already-written data. In that case, forward-fixing (shipping a small patch on top of the new version) is the safer path, even though it feels slower.

slides.sectionTitle: A rolling deploy that breaks itself
slides.markdown:
A team ships a migration that adds a `NOT NULL` column in the same release as application code that writes it — as one combined deploy, with no expand/contract split. During the rolling deploy, old-version instances are still running side by side with new-version instances (this is how rolling deploys work: a mix of versions during the rollout window).

The old instances, unaware of the new column, insert rows without it — and the `NOT NULL` constraint rejects every one of those writes, causing a spike of errors *during the deploy itself*, not after. The team can't roll back cleanly either, because some rows now have the column populated and some don't, and neither app version handles that mixed state correctly.

A simplified automated-rollback rule tied to a canary stage:

```yaml
canary:
  traffic_percent: 5
  bake_time: 10m
  rollback_if:
    - metric: error_rate
      threshold: "> 2x baseline"
    - metric: p99_latency_ms
      threshold: "> 500"
    - metric: checkout_success_rate
      threshold: "< 98%"
  on_rollback:
    action: revert_to_previous_version
    notify: ["#incidents"]
```

Notice the thresholds mix infra metrics (error rate, latency) with a **business** metric (checkout success rate) — a purely infra-based check can miss a bug that doesn't throw errors or slow anything down, but does quietly break a business flow.

slides.sectionTitle: Rollback plans need a rehearsal, not just a runbook
slides.markdown:
A documented rollback procedure that's never been executed is a hypothesis, not a safety net. The common failure: the runbook says "redeploy the previous version," but the previous version's artifact was already garbage-collected from the registry's retention policy, or the previous version's config has since drifted and no longer matches what's actually needed to run it.

Teams that treat rollback as a first-class capability test it periodically — a scheduled rollback drill, or requiring every deploy pipeline to prove a rollback path works as part of its own validation — rather than discovering the gap during a real incident, under pressure, when it matters most.

slides.sectionTitle: Design for reversal, not just for correctness
slides.markdown:
The mindset shift this topic asks for: don't just ask "will this deploy work?" — ask "if it doesn't, how do I undo it, and how long will that take?" That second question should be answered *before* the deploy starts, not improvised after.

The schema-migration case is the sharpest version of this: rollback safety has to be designed into the migration itself (expand/contract), because no amount of deploy tooling rescues a rollback once incompatible data already exists. Build & Dependency Management is the companion topic — reproducible builds are what make "redeploy the previous version" mean something precise in the first place.
